<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This report resolves several questions left open by the earlier documents, and it does so mostly with appropriate caution. The arithmetic checks out. On the earlier disputes, it is right that "entirely an artifact" is refuted by its own data. It is also right that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies cannot speak to decay. It even confirms that all four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which explains why their pooled estimate looked undecayed.

Two problems matter more than the rest:

1. The control group was contaminated midway, which muddies the decay estimate.
2. The mediation result is described more strongly than its design supports.

## What checks out

- **24-month per-hour figures:** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5% on logs.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 is a 13.4% fall in hours, and 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8% per hour.
- **Meeting time:** treated 7.4 → 3.9 and control 7.2 → 7.0. These match the month-six levels in the nine-month report (3.8 v 7.1), so the series is consistent.
- **Survivorship caveat:** the Halden continuers are correctly described as "survivors twice over".
- **Mediation assumptions:** the Limitations section correctly flags the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption.

## Main issues

### 1. Control offices changed their practices, which affects the decay estimate

The "unplanned observation" is presented as a side note. It is actually a contamination of the control arm, and it bears directly on the headline.

- At month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings. Their output per hour then rose 4.1%.
- Spread across seven offices, that alone lifts the control average by about 1.2%.
- Because the estimate is difference-in-differences, a rising control group shrinks the measured treatment effect.

So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control group improving, not the treated offices fading. The meeting audit may itself have been prompted by the trial's own meetings finding, which would make it spillover rather than coincidence.

The report should show:

- treated and control trajectories separately;
- the 24-month estimate with and without the two affected offices, or with only pre-month-15 control data as a sensitivity check.

As written, "the gain has declined" combines fading in treated offices with improvement in control offices.

### 2. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

The registered mediation test is a real improvement on the nine-month exploratory correlation. But it is not the independent confirmation the Summary implies.

- **Same units.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices and was tested on them again. Pre-registration guards against flexible analysis. It does not turn a re-test on the same units into a replication.
- **Office-months are not independent.** The independent units are still 7 treated and 7 control offices. Repeated observations add little information about *between-office* mediation. A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for an analysis resting on 14 clusters, and the method used to compute it should be reported.
- **Mediators weren't randomised.** Offices that cut meetings more may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's "confirms" doesn't reflect it.
- **The two mediators may not be separate.** Cutting meetings could reduce fatigue. If so, the 47% / 18% split depends on model specification and ordering. It would help to report whether the model allowed fatigue to be downstream of meetings.

"The meetings pathway is supported by a pre-registered test" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not.

### 3. It's unclear what the log-hours measure includes

The report defines log hours as "active log-in time on the case-management system". If that means time spent working on cases, it probably excludes meetings, since meetings happen off the case system. That creates two problems:

- **The −11% figure is hard to explain.** Total hours fell about 12%, and about 3.5 of the roughly 4.5 hours removed were meetings. Case-system time should then have fallen only around 3%, not 11%.
- **The mediation is harder to interpret.** If the outcome excludes meeting time, cutting meetings doesn't mechanically raise output per log-hour. The meetings pathway would then need a different mechanism, such as less fragmentation of the working day.

On the other hand, if logs include meetings, the arithmetic works. Then an accounting identity applies:

- Non-meeting hours fell from about 30.5 to 29.5, roughly −3%.
- Output per non-meeting hour is then about 0.966 / 0.967, essentially unchanged.

On that reading, nearly all of the per-hour gain is time removed from meetings, more than the 47% the mediation attributes to it. The definition of log hours needs to be stated precisely, because the two readings imply quite different conclusions about mechanism.

### 4. The Summary compares different hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". That compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The body correctly uses the like-for-like comparison, 12.5% → 9.8%.

The three descriptions of the decline don't match:

| Comparison | Relative decline |
|---|---|
| Timesheets to timesheets (body) | 22% |
| Timesheets to logs (Summary) | 32% |
| §5 wording | "about a quarter" |

The Summary should use the timesheet-to-timesheet figure, with the log estimate given separately.

### 5. The marketing agency doesn't fit "client-facing or coverage obligations"

The marketing agency reverted citing client deadlines. In the meta-analysis's coding, and in this literature's framework generally, deadline-driven work is the definition of *discretionary* work. Calling it "client-facing" to group it with the retail and hospitality reversions makes the evidence fit the work-type framework more neatly than it does. It's more informative as a counterexample: one discretionary organisation in 11 found the model unworkable.

## Smaller points

- **Counter-arm cost.** 12% more staff raising cost per contact by 9% is plausible if labour is about three-quarters of total cost. The calculation should be shown.
- **Halden baseline hours.** The 11 continuing organisations have baseline hours of 40.3. That is exactly the 27-organisation mean in Varga and Holm. It may be a coincidence, but it's worth checking it wasn't carried over.
- **Halden response rate.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. Non-response is likely related to how things went, which adds a third layer of selection beyond completing and continuing.
- **Sick days and resignations.** These still lack confidence intervals, as at nine months.
- **Protocol timing.** The follow-up protocol was filed at month 11, after the nine-month results were known. That is normal, but the choice to add the log measure and the mediators was informed by interim data, and the report should say so.
- **Conflict of interest.** One author (Okafor) wrote the original Halden paper, and the Varden authors are testing their own hypothesis. This doesn't invalidate anything, but it makes independent replication of the meetings result more valuable.

## Where the six documents now leave things

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Halden's +23.4% headline | Substantially inflated by the scheduled-hours denominator, manager reporting and survivor attrition |
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Real and modest: about 8–12% on strong measures, declining somewhat over two years |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly below baseline (about −2% to −3%); the CI includes losses of up to about 8% |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall. Varden ended its arm at month 12, at a projected 9% higher cost per contact to restore service |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Refuted for measurement and selection. The novelty question is partly answered: some fading, nowhere near zero |
| "No sign of decay" | Unsupported, since it rested on four studies with inflating designs |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the leading candidate, possibly most of the gain, but it rests on 7 offices plus 2 uncontrolled ones |

The most important open question is the one the report itself identifies: whether reorganisation **without** an hours cut captures most of the gain. If meetings account for most of it, an arm that reorganises at full hours is the obvious next trial. It would separate "shorter hours raise productivity" from "shorter hours force reorganisation that raises productivity".

I can draft the sensitivity analysis for the control contamination, or a design for the reorganisation-only trial.
